issues.legal_issue: A state legislature may annul transfers of agricultural land made by members of a protected tribal community and restore the land to them under its power over agricultural land.
material_facts: The legislation provided for restoration of agricultural land transferred by tribal owners to non-tribal transferees during a specified period, subject to repayment and adjustment for improvements and encumbrances.
A government-appointed committee reported that existing safeguards had failed to prevent the exploitation and dispossession of tribal landholders.
The challenged transfers involved agricultural land, and the restoration scheme required the tribal transferor to undertake personal cultivation and make specified payments to the transferee.
issues.conclusion: The law was within the state legislature’s competence because it concerned transfers and alienations of agricultural land, including the power to reopen such transfers and provide for restitution.
issues.legal_principle: Entry 18 of List II covers transfers and alienations of agricultural land and empowers a state legislature not only to restrict or prohibit such transfers but also to reopen them. Entries 6 and 7 of List III exclude agricultural land from their respective fields. The Court treated the law as an instrument of distributive justice aimed at correcting exploitation and unequal bargaining power, referring to Manchegowda v. State of Karnataka, Fateh Chand Himmatlal v. State of Maharashtra, and Pathumma v. State of Kerala.

predicates.state_legislative_competence_challenge: The case challenges whether a state legislature had authority to enact a law governing the transfer of land.
predicates.land_is_agricultural: The land governed by the challenged law is agricultural land.
predicates.transfer_involves_protected_tribal_owner: The transfer governed by the law was made by a member of a specially protected tribal community.

issues.definition: When a challenge concerns state authority over a transfer of agricultural land made by a protected tribal owner, the state legislature has power to enact a law reopening the transfer and restoring the land.

issues.legal_issue: A law protected by constitutional placement in the Ninth Schedule cannot be invalidated on the ground that it is inconsistent with or abridges the fundamental rights specified in Article 31B.
material_facts: The challenged enactment had been placed in the Ninth Schedule of the Constitution.
The challengers argued that its provisions violated Articles 14, 19(1)(f), and 31.
issues.conclusion: The fundamental-rights challenge had to be rejected because Article 31B protected the enactment from that challenge.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31B protects laws included in the Ninth Schedule from invalidation on the ground that they are inconsistent with, take away, or abridge rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: The case challenges the constitutional validity of an enactment.
predicates.enactment_has_ninth_schedule_protection: The enactment has the constitutional protection associated with inclusion in the Ninth Schedule.
predicates.challenge_relies_on_protected_fundamenta: The challenge asserts inconsistency with or abridgment of fundamental rights covered by the constitutional protection.

issues.definition: A constitutional challenge based on protected fundamental rights is barred when the challenged enactment has Ninth Schedule protection.

issues.legal_issue: A legislature may use a past date to define the reach of a law when the date has a reasonable connection to the law’s objective.
material_facts: The law made transfers from a selected past date eligible for annulment and restoration.
That date was the date on which tenant purchasers could seek to acquire their holdings under the relevant tenancy regime.
The challengers argued that the selected date was arbitrary.
issues.conclusion: The selected date was not arbitrary because it had a reasonable nexus to the object of the legislation.
issues.legal_principle: A legislature may classify by time if there is a reasonable nexus between the temporal line and the object sought to be achieved. The Court relied on the connection between the selected date and the commencement of tenant purchasers’ ability to seek purchase of their holdings under the relevant tenancy law.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_temporal_cla: The case challenges a law’s use of a past date to determine which events fall within its operation.
predicates.cutoff_date_has_reasonable_connection_to: The selected date is connected to a legal or practical circumstance relevant to the objective of the law.

issues.definition: A challenged temporal classification is valid when the selected date is reasonably connected to the law’s objective.

issues.legal_issue: Treating members of a protected tribal community differently from members of another disadvantaged community does not invalidate a law when the tribal community is a distinct class requiring special protection.
material_facts: The law provided a restorative remedy for transfers made by members of a tribal community but not for transfers made by members of Scheduled Castes.
The challengers were transferees from tribal owners and sought to rely on the alleged disadvantage to members of Scheduled Castes.
The Court regarded tribal communities, many of whom were aboriginal, as a distinct class requiring special state protection.
issues.conclusion: The distinction did not violate Article 14, and the challengers could not plead the cause of members of Scheduled Castes.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 permits differential treatment based on a rational distinction. The Court held that tribal communities constituted a distinct class requiring special protection and that transferees from tribal owners could not assert the cause of members of another community.

predicates.equal_protection_challenge: The case alleges that a law treats similarly situated groups unequally.
predicates.tribal_community_is_distinct_protected_c: The group receiving the law’s protection is a distinct community with a particular need for special protection.
predicates.challengers_are_transferees_from_that_cl: The challengers acquired property from members of the protected community and seek to contest the law’s treatment of another disadvantaged group.

issues.definition: A transferee from a distinct protected tribal class cannot invalidate the law on the ground that another disadvantaged group does not receive the same remedy.

issues.legal_issue: Excluding land that has been put to a non-agricultural use from a restorative regime for agricultural land does not create an unconstitutional distinction from land that remains agricultural.
material_facts: The law provided for restoration of agricultural land transferred by tribal owners.
The challengers compared transferees who had put land to non-agricultural use with transferees who continued to use land agriculturally.

The Court reasoned that land put to a non-agricultural use had ceased to be agricultural land and that state authority over agricultural land did not extend to the same restorative measure for such land without the required constitutional process.
issues.conclusion: The distinction did not violate Article 14 because land put to non-agricultural use was not similarly situated to land that remained agricultural.
issues.legal_principle: The state’s power over agricultural land does not extend to a restorative law for land that has ceased to be agricultural merely because it was once agricultural. A law concerning such non-agricultural land would require the relevant constitutional process, including reservation for and receipt of presidential assent, as applicable.

predicates.equal_protection_challenge: The case alleges that a law treats similarly situated groups unequally.
predicates.restorative_law_is_limited_to_agricultur: The challenged restorative regime applies to land while it remains agricultural.
predicates.compared_land_has_been_put_to_nonagricul: The land used for comparison has been converted to a non-agricultural purpose.

issues.definition: Different treatment is not unequal treatment of equals when the restorative regime covers agricultural land but the compared land has been put to a non-agricultural use.

issues.legal_issue: An inclusive definition of a non-tribal transferee does not allow a later assignee to escape the restorative regime merely because the assignment occurred before the date chosen to give the law retrospective effect.
material_facts: The law defined a non-tribal transferee inclusively to include successors-in-interest.
The challengers argued that an assignee who acquired land before the date on which the government began its inquiry would escape the consequences of restoration.
The Court read the definition and the scheme as covering a transferee or successor who made a later transfer on or after that date.
issues.conclusion: The definition did not permit an assignee to escape the consequences of the restorative law in the manner argued by the challengers.
issues.legal_principle: An inclusive statutory definition is read consistently with the scheme of the enactment. The Court treated the inquiry’s commencement as the point chosen for retrospective operation and construed the definition to include successors who transferred the land on or after that point.

predicates.interpretation_challenge_to_restorative_: The case disputes how a restorative law applies to a transferee or successor in interest.
predicates.transferee_definition_includes_successor: The law’s definition of a transferee encompasses successors in interest.
predicates.successor_made_later_transfer_after_inqu: A successor in interest made a further transfer after the government had begun the inquiry that led to the restorative measure.

issues.definition: A successor included in the transferee definition is not exempt on the asserted ground when that successor made a further transfer after the inquiry began.

issues.legal_issue: A restriction on advocates appearing in specified administrative restoration proceedings does not unconstitutionally restrict an advocate’s professional right when the asserted general right of audience has not been brought into force.
material_facts: The law barred pleaders from appearing for parties in proceedings before administrative revenue authorities under the restorative regime.
The advocates relied on their enrolment and on a statutory provision conferring a general right to practise, but that provision had not been brought into force.
The Court stated that the applicable right to practise remained governed by the law then in force.
issues.conclusion: The bar on advocates appearing in those proceedings was not an unconstitutional restriction on their right to practise their profession.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Advocates Act, 1961, section 30 did not confer an operative general right of audience because it had not been brought into force. The right to practise was governed by the applicable provisions of the Bar Councils Act, 1926, including section 14(1)(a), (b), and (c).

predicates.challenge_to_professional_practice_restr: The case challenges a restriction on advocates appearing in a category of proceedings.
predicates.advocate_general_audience_right_not_in_f: The asserted general right of audience had not been made operative.
predicates.restriction_applies_to_specific_administ: The appearance restriction is confined to proceedings before administrative decision-makers under a particular remedial scheme.

issues.definition: A restriction confined to specified administrative proceedings does not unconstitutionally restrict an advocate’s professional right when the asserted general right of audience is not operative.

issues.legal_issue: A litigant has no fundamental right to be represented by a lawyer in non-criminal administrative proceedings, apart from the constitutional right of an accused who is arrested and detained to consult and be defended by a lawyer of choice.
material_facts: The law barred legal representatives from appearing for parties in the specified administrative restoration proceedings, subject to limited exceptions for persons under disability.
The challengers argued that they had a right to representation by a legal practitioner of their choice.
The proceedings were not criminal proceedings involving an accused arrested and detained in custody.
The Court considered the need to complete the proceedings promptly and restore land without delay.
issues.conclusion: The litigants had no fundamental right to representation by a lawyer in those proceedings, and the restriction was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Article 22(1) recognizes the right of an accused who is arrested and detained in custody to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of choice. Outside that situation, a litigant has no fundamental right to legal representation in court or other proceedings. The Court also accepted that restricting lawyers’ appearances could serve the public interest by preventing delay in proceedings intended to restore land promptly.

rule.if: challenge_to_lawyer_representation_bar and noncriminal_administrative_proceeding and party_not_arrested_and_detained_on_criminal_charge and proceeding_requires_prompt_completion

predicates.challenge_to_lawyer_representation_bar: The case challenges a rule that prevents a litigant from being represented by a lawyer.
predicates.noncriminal_administrative_proceeding: The challenged proceeding is an administrative proceeding and is not a criminal prosecution.
predicates.party_not_arrested_and_detained_on_crimi: The litigant is not an accused arrested and detained in custody on a criminal charge.
predicates.proceeding_requires_prompt_completion: The proceeding is intended to be completed promptly to deliver the remedial outcome without delay.

issues.definition: In a non-criminal administrative proceeding requiring prompt completion, a litigant who is not an arrested and detained accused has no fundamental right to lawyer representation.
